name: DEM and bathymetry for separating desilting from encroachment

identity.method_name: Public digital elevation models (USGS/SRTMGL1_003, JAXA/ALOS/AW3D30/V4_1, CartoDEM, Copernicus GLO-30) and DEM-derived stage-area-volume (hypsometric) bathymetry reconstruction, cross-checked against ICESat-2 ATL13 inland water surface heights
identity.core_idea: The idea being tested is that desilting (excavation that deepens a tank without permanently removing its surface footprint) and encroachment (permanent conversion of lakebed/buffer to built structures) should be separable if a second, later elevation survey shows the lakebed got DEEPER while the shoreline stayed roughly the SAME, versus a case where the shoreline itself retreats permanently. In practice this requires either (a) two independently-dated DEMs of adequate vertical accuracy to difference, or (b) a DEM-derived hypsometric stage-area-volume curve built by intersecting multi-date satellite water extent with the exposed-bed elevation, which lets water AREA time series (already collected by this project) be converted into an estimated water VOLUME/depth time series without a second DEM date. Both routes are tested here against the public DEMs realistically obtainable for Bengaluru, plus ICESat-2 ATL13 as a possible independent water-level check.
identity.official_dataset_ids: USGS/SRTMGL1_003 (SRTM GL1, 1 arc-second / ~30 m void-filled global DEM, Google Earth Engine / LP DAAC catalog ID, exact as given). JAXA/ALOS/AW3D30/V4_1 (ALOS World 3D - 30m, version 4.1, Google Earth Engine catalog ID, exact as given). CartoDEM: no official Earth Engine / STAC dataset ID exists; distributed by NRSC/ISRO as 'CartoDEM' (versions V1 through V3.1/R1 across successive reprocessing rounds) via the Bhuvan portal (bhuvan-app3.nrsc.gov.in), not indexed in any public machine-readable catalog [verify exact current version string, not confirmed this session due to a portal connection error]. Copernicus DEM GLO-30, product ID COPERNICUS/DEM/GLO30 on Google Earth Engine (added here as the one other realistically obtainable 30 m global DEM, derived from TanDEM-X, generally regarded as more accurate than SRTM/AW3D30/CartoDEM) [verify exact GEE asset id string]. ICESat-2 ATL13, 'Along Track Inland Surface Water Data', distributed via NASA NSIDC DAAC; this research directly confirmed via the NSIDC product page that Version 006 has been retired in favour of a newer Version 007 as of this research date (September 2026) [verify exact current version number and DOI at time of use, e.g. pattern 10.5067/ATLAS/ATL13.0XX]. sciencedirect S0034425723005126 (DEM-derived inundated bathymetry reconstruction paper referenced in the task note): full text and abstract were paywall-blocked (HTTP 403) in this research session; title, authors, exact methodology and study area could NOT be confirmed against the primary source and are reported here only as [uncertain] based on the paper's likely subject area inferred from its Elsevier pii pattern (Remote Sensing of Environment, 2023 volume) and the task note's own description.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Not a labelling strategy in the supervised-learning sense; DEM/bathymetry data is a covariate/diagnostic input meant to help disambiguate two competing explanations (desilting vs. encroachment) for an observed change in the project's own water-area/footprint series, not to produce an encroachment label itself. The finding below is that none of the realistically obtainable public DEMs can actually perform this disambiguation for these lakes, so its practical value as a proxy is effectively zero; the note's own suggested fallback -- documentary evidence (BBMP/BWSSB desilting tender records, works orders, contemporaneous news coverage) obtained by manual per-lake-year search -- is the recommended real source, and that is a manual-annotation strategy, not a remote-sensing one, costing roughly 0.5-1 student-day per lake per suspected desilting event to search and document.
fit_to_project.input_required: A bare-earth or bathymetric DEM covering each lake and its immediate buffer, ideally with two independently-dated epochs to difference, in the project's EPSG:32643 grid. The project currently has none of this (only the OSM boundary and Sentinel-2 optical bands). SRTM, AW3D30 and CartoDEM are all free to obtain (CartoDEM requires Bhuvan registration); Copernicus GLO-30 is free with no registration; ICESat-2 ATL13 granules require a free NASA Earthdata login. Acquiring any of these costs at most a few hours; the finding below is that acquiring them does not solve the stated problem, not that they are hard to obtain.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: no, regardless of how the 42 rows are reframed. Elevation from a single-epoch DEM is a static, non-varying value per pixel, so joining it to the lake-year table adds only 6 constant values (one per lake), contributing zero year-to-year signal -- the exact same failure mode the project's own limitations section already documents for OpenStreetMap buildings. Reframing to the hypsometric stage-area-volume approach (regressing the project's own 42 water-area observations against a DEM-derived elevation-to-area curve) is technically a per-scene, n=42 computation, but the underlying physics does not support it here: these are shallow engineered tanks with roughly 1-3 m of usable bed relief (typical urban-tank depth and typical silt-removal depth during desilting), which is smaller than the vertical error of every public DEM considered here (commonly cited absolute vertical accuracy figures are on the order of 5-16 m for SRTM, roughly 5 m for AW3D30, and roughly 8-10 m for CartoDEM -- each figure [verify], but even the best of them approaches or exceeds the target signal). The row count is not the constraint; the vertical measurement precision is.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes in the narrow sense that no encroachment labels are needed to acquire or difference a DEM -- but this is close to a moot point, because the method does not achieve its intended purpose here even without any labelling requirement. The recommended substitute (documentary evidence) is itself a form of manual annotation, not label-free.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Raster DEMs (SRTM, AW3D30, CartoDEM, Copernicus GLO-30) are all nominally ~30 m, close enough to the project's 20 m grid to resample without difficulty -- resolution match is not the problem. ICESat-2 ATL13 is not a raster at all; it is a sparse set of along-track photon-derived height segments (typically tens of metres long) following six fixed narrow ground tracks, fundamentally mismatched to a regular 20 m grid and unusable as a gridded covariate without heavy, likely data-starved, interpolation (see the ATL13 finding below). No sub-metre or LiDAR DEM with genuine multi-date coverage of these lakes was found to be realistically obtainable by a solo student (see temporal_granularity).
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: None for the DEM approach itself (it is unsupervised, purely geometric). The item's own honest conclusion is that the real disambiguation source should instead be documentary evidence -- BBMP/BWSSB desilting tender awards, works orders, contractor mobilisation records, and contemporaneous local news coverage of desilting at named lakes -- collected manually per lake-year, which functions as a weak/manual label for 'desilting was underway in year Y' rather than as elevation data.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: None of the four numbered limitations directly (only 42 rows; OpenStreetMap is a single snapshot; no real ground truth; one dry-season scene per year). This item targets the separate, though equally central, confound_desilting problem named in the project's own constraints (Bellandur's 15.7 ha -> 0.4 ha -> 107.9 ha swing). If forced onto the four-item list, it has the weakest secondary link to limitation (3) 'no real ground truth', since resolving the desilting confound would make any water-area-based proxy label more trustworthy -- but the finding below is that DEM data cannot deliver that, so even this secondary link does not materialise.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No -- this is the central, brutally honest finding of this item. SRTM is a single radar overflight from 11-22 February 2000 and by definition cannot show any change across the project's 2019-2025 window; AW3D30's version history (V1.1 through V4.1) is reprocessing and void-filling of the SAME underlying ALOS PRISM stereo imagery acquired circa 2006-2011, not new dates, so a later version number does not mean a later elevation date [verify exact PRISM acquisition window]; CartoDEM is likewise built from a fixed Cartosat-1 stereo campaign window [verify exact years, not confirmed this session] and is not resurveyed; Copernicus GLO-30 is a single epoch from TanDEM-X data acquired roughly 2011-2015 [verify]. No multi-date, open elevation product spanning 2019-2025 at any usable vertical accuracy was found to exist for these lakes. Even if a second epoch existed, the DEM-derived hypsometric approach fails at the vertical-relief scale of these shallow tanks (see viable_with_42_rows). ICESat-2 ATL13 (2018-present, repeating) is in principle a real multi-date water-level source, but its six narrow, widely-spaced ground tracks make usable returns over lakes of 12-315 ha essentially a matter of chance rather than design (see risk/evidence): most of these lakes are small enough in at least one dimension that no ATL13 ground track can be assumed to cross them at all during the mission life, and this research found no confirmed ATL13 validation study targeting lakes this small. CONCLUSION, stated plainly as the task requires: the desilting-vs-encroachment confound CANNOT be resolved by any elevation data realistically obtainable for this project, and must instead be resolved by documentary evidence (desilting tender records, BBMP/BWSSB works orders, contemporaneous news) collected per lake-year.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No. Elevation data says nothing about the spectral difference between open water and floating water-hyacinth mats; this confound remains entirely a job for the optical/spectral methods elsewhere in this research programme (e.g. the MDPI Remote Sensing 2020 macrophyte mapping cross-check).
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None of the DEM sources carries any legal or cadastral standing over the lake boundary or footprint; they are purely geometric/elevation products. Note the inversion this creates: the RECOMMENDED alternative (documentary evidence of a desilting tender or BBMP/BWSSB works order) is, incidentally, MORE legally traceable than any remote-sensing signal considered anywhere in this research programme, because a works order or tender award is itself an administrative/legal record of an authorised activity -- this makes the documentary-evidence route doubly preferable: it is the only route that can resolve the confound at all, AND it happens to produce a more defensible evidentiary trail than a DEM difference ever could.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Worse than the project's already-flagged OpenStreetMap-snapshot problem, and worth stating explicitly: SRTM is fixed at a single 11-day window in February 2000 and will never have a second date under any version number. AW3D30's apparent 'versions' (V1.1 -> V2.1 -> V2.2 -> V3.1 -> V3.2 -> V4.1) are software/void-fill reprocessing of one fixed ALOS PRISM acquisition window and do not add a new elevation date [verify acquisition window precisely]. CartoDEM's versions are likewise reprocessing of one fixed Cartosat-1 stereo campaign [verify]. Copernicus GLO-30 is one fixed TanDEM-X epoch [verify]. None of the four raster DEMs varies year to year at all -- at least OpenStreetMap COULD in principle be manually re-edited by the student to reflect a later date; these DEMs cannot be updated to a new date without commissioning fresh stereo or LiDAR acquisition, which is far outside a solo student's budget and timeline. ICESat-2 ATL13 is the one genuinely time-varying elevation source in this list (2018-present, repeating ~91-day orbit), but see handles_desilting_confound for why its coverage of lakes this small is likely to be sparse-to-absent in practice.

implementation.libraries: rasterio, GDAL, richdem or whitebox_workflows (hydrological/terrain processing), earthengine-api (to pull USGS/SRTMGL1_003, JAXA/ALOS/AW3D30/V4_1 and COPERNICUS/DEM/GLO30 without local downloads), h5py or icepyx (ICESat-2 ATL13 HDF5 granule access and along-track filtering), geopandas for zonal/point-in-polygon extraction.
implementation.pretrained_weights: not applicable -- these are raw elevation/altimetry data products, not trained models.
implementation.licence: SRTM (USGS/NASA): public domain, no restriction. ALOS AW3D30 (JAXA): free for research and educational use after registration; commercial redistribution restricted [verify exact current terms]. CartoDEM (NRSC/ISRO, via Bhuvan): free for non-commercial/academic use after registration; redistribution restricted [verify]. Copernicus DEM GLO-30: open, free, ESA/Airbus terms, attribution requested. ICESat-2 ATL13 (NASA/NSIDC): public domain, free after a no-cost NASA Earthdata login. None of this poses a licence problem for an academic capstone.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial and CPU-only. The raster DEMs covering a 22x17 km study area at 30 m are only a few megabytes; zonal statistics and any differencing run in seconds on a laptop. Searching and filtering ICESat-2 ATL13 granules by geolocation over 6 small polygons across 2018-present is more tedious than compute-intensive -- a scripting task of a few hours, likely to return an empty or near-empty result given the geometry problem described above. No GPU, Colab, or Earth Engine quota concern exists for this item.
implementation.student_days: DEM acquisition and a sanity-check comparison across SRTM/AW3D30/CartoDEM/Copernicus GLO-30: 1-2 days. ICESat-2 ATL13 granule search and extraction, to confirm (most likely) that no usable returns exist over the 6 study lakes: 1-2 days, budgeted explicitly as a check expected to produce a null result rather than a feature pipeline. The recommended documentary-evidence alternative: roughly 0.5-1 day per lake per suspected desilting episode to search BBMP/BWSSB tender portals, news archives and any available works-order records, so for the project's 6 lakes across 7 years, budget on the order of 3-6 student-days total, treated as an ongoing manual research task rather than a coding deliverable.

evaluation.metrics: Not a predictive model, so no accuracy/F1-style metric applies directly. If a second DEM epoch or the hypsometric approach were used, the relevant metric would be the elevation-difference residual (metres) compared against the known vertical error of each DEM, to show whether any detected 'change' exceeds instrument noise -- the finding above is that it generally would not. For the recommended documentary-evidence route, the useful measure is qualitative corroboration coverage: the fraction of lake-years with a suspected large area change for which a matching desilting record (tender, works order, or news report) could or could not be found.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Not applicable in the machine-learning sense -- no model is being fit here. If DEM-derived features were ever added as a static covariate to a downstream panel model (e.g. item C3's mixed-effects model), that model's own leave-one-lake-out protocol would apply, unchanged.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Minimal for the DEM data itself (static, unlikely to leak information about the target). The real leakage risk sits in the recommended documentary-evidence alternative: a desilting news report or tender record effectively already reveals the answer being investigated, so it must be used strictly as an ANNOTATION/LABEL source for a given lake-year (i.e. to correctly classify that lake-year as 'known desilting' before evaluating any water-area-based method), never as an input feature fed into the same water-based method whose job is to detect the change independently -- doing so would be direct label leakage.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: If a hypsometric regression were attempted despite the finding above, the DEM's own vertical error (5-16 m, per-source figures [verify]) should be explicitly propagated into any resulting volume/depth estimate; doing so honestly would produce an uncertainty band far wider than the signal being measured, which is itself the clearest quantitative demonstration of why this approach should be abandoned rather than reported with a misleadingly precise point estimate. The documentary-evidence route produces no numeric uncertainty interval, only a qualitative confidence tier per lake-year (primary record found / secondary news report found / no record found).
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: not applicable -- no synthetic data generation is involved in either the DEM approach or the documentary-evidence alternative.

evidence.published_performance: Commonly cited specification/validation figures, none independently re-verified against a primary accuracy-assessment paper in this session and therefore all marked [verify]: SRTM absolute vertical accuracy specification of <16 m (90% linear error) globally, with published regional validation studies often reporting better RMSE (roughly 5-10 m) in low-relief terrain [verify]. AW3D30 JAXA-reported vertical accuracy on the order of 5 m RMSE [verify; the JAXA AW3D30 product page itself could not be reached in this session due to a connection error]. CartoDEM NRSC-reported vertical accuracy on the order of 8-10 m RMSE [verify; the Bhuvan portal could not be reached in this session]. Copernicus GLO-30 is generally reported in the literature as more accurate than the above (commonly cited absolute vertical accuracy on the order of 2-4 m) [verify]. For sciencedirect S0034425723005126, the paper's own reported performance figures could not be retrieved (403 paywall) and are [uncertain] in full. The single load-bearing quantitative comparison this item can make with confidence is qualitative, not a specific digit: EVERY one of these DEM vertical-error figures is on the same order of magnitude as, or larger than, the 1-3 m of bed relief typical of a desilted shallow urban tank, which is sufficient by itself to support the negative conclusion regardless of which exact accuracy figure is used.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: SRTM, AW3D30, CartoDEM and Copernicus GLO-30 are global or national products, not validated specifically for Bengaluru's small engineered tanks. The DEM-derived hypsometric bathymetry-reconstruction technique referenced in the task note (sciencedirect S0034425723005126) could not be confirmed for its study area in this session (paywalled), but this class of technique, based on general domain knowledge of the published literature, is typically demonstrated on large reservoirs and natural lakes spanning tens to thousands of km2 with metres-to-tens-of-metres of seasonal stage variation -- a materially different regime from Bengaluru's 12-315 ha tanks with roughly 1-3 m of relevant depth variation. Applying a technique validated at that scale to these lakes without re-validation would itself be a scale-mismatch error of exactly the kind this research programme is designed to catch.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No confirmed study was found in this research applying SRTM/AW3D30/CartoDEM/Copernicus-GLO-30-based bathymetric change detection specifically to Bengaluru's lakes. The sibling research item on authoritative boundary sources (B2) found that IISc's Energy & Wetlands Research Group (T V Ramachandra et al.), the most active academic group studying Bengaluru's lakes, is reported to rely on Survey of India toposheets plus field/differential GPS survey rather than DEM differencing [uncertain, based on aggregated search-result summaries, not a directly confirmed quoted methods passage] -- this is at least consistent with DEM-based depth-change detection not being an established method for these lakes in the existing literature.
evidence.evidence_recency: AW3D30 V4.1 is a 2021-era reprocessing release of imagery from 2006-2011 [verify]; CartoDEM's most recent public version is roughly 2015-era processing of imagery up to about 2014 [verify]; SRTM's void-filled SRTMGL1_003 product itself was last updated circa 2015 but the underlying radar data is fixed at February 2000 and can never be newer. ICESat-2 (launched 2018) is an active, ongoing mission and this research directly confirmed via the NSIDC product page that ATL13 Version 006 has been retired in favour of a newer Version 007 as of September 2026 -- so the ALTIMETRY SOURCE is current, even though its practical usability over small lakes is the separate finding above. Overall: dataset PROCESSING recency is generally fine; it is irrelevant to the underlying finding, because the source elevation EPOCHS themselves remain frozen in the past regardless of software reprocessing date.

risk.failure_modes: (1) Treating routine DEM vertical noise (a few metres) as a genuine excavation or footprint signal, fabricating a false desilting-vs-encroachment conclusion from data that cannot actually resolve it. (2) Assuming a newer AW3D30 or CartoDEM VERSION NUMBER implies a newer elevation DATE, when it is only reprocessing of the same fixed historical stereo imagery -- a common and easy misunderstanding that would falsely claim multi-temporal capability that does not exist. (3) Spending real effort searching ICESat-2 ATL13 granules without first budgeting for the likely outcome of zero or near-zero usable returns over lakes this small, and only discovering that after the time is already spent. (4) Citing the sciencedirect S0034425723005126 paper's technique or figures without having actually read past its paywall, and without checking that its study area/scale (likely large reservoirs) matches these small urban tanks.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask, directly: 'can you actually measure whether that lake got shallower?' The honest, defensible answer supported by the evidence gathered here is NO -- every public DEM covering these lakes is either a single frozen historical epoch (SRTM: fixed at February 2000) or a product whose later version numbers are reprocessing, not new imagery (AW3D30, CartoDEM, Copernicus GLO-30), and none has vertical precision finer than the roughly 1-3 m of depth change involved in desilting a shallow urban tank. That is a genuinely defensible null result PROVIDED it is stated plainly, with the reasoning above, rather than glossed over by presenting a DEM-based analysis that implies more precision than the data actually has.
risk.honest_expectation: DEM and satellite-altimetry data will NOT resolve the desilting-vs-encroachment confound for this project. The realistic, honestly reportable outcome is a documented negative finding, exactly as reasoned above, followed by a pivot to documentary evidence (BBMP/BWSSB desilting tender and works-order records, and contemporaneous news coverage) as the actual disambiguation method, applied manually per lake-year rather than through a remote-sensing pipeline. A null result stated this clearly is itself a legitimate and useful contribution of this research item.

verdict.recommended_rank: reject -- as a remote-sensing method for resolving the desilting confound, given that no multi-date elevation product of adequate vertical accuracy exists for these lakes. adopt-if-time as a brief due-diligence step: spend 1-2 days confirming this negative finding directly (a quick ICESat-2 ATL13 granule check over the 6 lakes, and a one-time SRTM/AW3D30 sanity comparison) before committing fully to the documentary-evidence route, which should itself be rated adopt given it is the only route that can actually address this confound.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: No multi-date elevation dataset exists at a vertical accuracy finer than the roughly 1-3 m signal involved in desilting these lakes, so the desilting-versus-encroachment confound cannot be resolved with DEM or ICESat-2 data and is instead addressed with documentary evidence (BBMP/BWSSB desilting tender and works-order records, and contemporaneous news coverage) collected per lake-year.
